articles.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro (Highspeed) now available on Amazon Bedrock
articles.excerpt: Today, Kimi K3.1 Pro from Moonshot AI is available on Amazon Bedrock, expanding our open weight model portfolio with the security and governance that customers rely on. Customers using Amazon Bedrock can now run agentic use cases such as coding and document processing on Kimi K3.1 Pro (Highspeed), which delivers high output tokens per second (OTPS) for faster, more responsive results. According to Moonshot AI, Kimi K3.1 Pro is an open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model with a 1-million-token context window, and its most capable 3-trillion-parameter-class model to date. Moonshot AI reports improvements in coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic work. On Amazon Bedrock, it runs within the same security boundary as proprietary models and supports explicit prompt caching to reduce latency and input costs. Kimi K3.1 Pro is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock is available through cross-Region inference. To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock console . To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation .
articles.summary: Kimi K3.1 Pro (Highspeed) disponible sur Amazon Bedrock pour des cas d'usage agentiques avec sécurité, haute performance et contexte étendu.

articles.title: Agent Registry is now generally available in AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region
articles.excerpt: AWS Agent Registry, available through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is now available in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region. AWS Agent Registry is a fully managed discovery service that gives your organization a central catalog for organizing, curating, and discovering resources. You can publish MCP servers, tools, agents, agent skills, and custom resources to a searchable registry, and control what becomes discoverable through an approval workflow. People and AI agents can then find the right tools and agents through hybrid search, catalog browsing, and a native MCP endpoint. With Agent Registry in AWS GovCloud (US-West), public sector organizations and their partners get a single governed inventory of the agents and tools in their environment. Approval workflows and AWS CloudTrail audit logs support their compliance and oversight requirements. To get started, see the AWS Agent Registry documentation .
articles.summary: AWS Agent Registry est désormais disponible dans AWS GovCloud (US-West) pour centraliser et gouverner les agents/tools MCP avec auditabilité et conformité pour le secteur public.

articles.title: Any agent anywhere: How to use Grafana Cloud with Claude, Cursor, and any other AI agent
articles.excerpt: AI agents are becoming part of everyday engineering workflows, helping teams write code, troubleshoot issues, and automate tasks. But to be truly useful in production, these agents need access to more than code. They also need observability data and context to understand what's happening across your systems, investigate problems, and help you take action. At Grafana Labs, we believe that context should be available wherever you work. That’s one of the core ideas behind Grafana Cloud as the open agentic observability platform: the flexibility to work with your observability data through the AI agents you prefer—whether it’s Grafana Assistant , a coding agent in your IDE, or a tool you’ve built yourself—so you can investigate and troubleshoot issues without switching tools. In this post, we'll explore how to bring Grafana Cloud into your agentic workflows using tools like the Grafana Cloud MCP server and gcx , with practical examples along the way. You can also check out our ObservabilityCON 2026 talk in the video below to learn more. Three ways to use Grafana Cloud with AI agents There are multiple ways to bring Grafana Cloud observability data and context into your AI workflows, depending on where and how you prefer to work: Work directly in Grafana Cloud: Use Grafana Assistant, the AI-powered assistant built into Grafana Cloud, to investigate issues and interact with your observability data. Connect your preferred AI agent: Use the Grafana Cloud MCP server to bring Grafana Cloud data into compatible tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Codex. Work with coding agents and scripts: Use gcx, the Grafana Cloud command-line tool, to give coding agents access to observability data directly from their working environment. Whether you're working directly in Grafana Cloud with Grafana Assistant or using your own AI agents, you can choose the approach that works best for you. articles.title: Amazon MSK Replicator is now available in AWS GovCloud (US-East, US-West) Regions
articles.excerpt: You can now use Amazon MSK Replicator in the AWS GovCloud (US-East, US-West) Regions to replicate streaming data across Amazon MSK clusters and from external Apache Kafka clusters including on-premises, self-managed on AWS, or other cloud providers to Amazon MSK Provisioned clusters. MSK Replicator is a feature of Amazon MSK that automates data replication between Kafka clusters, eliminating the need to manage custom replication infrastructure or configure open-source tools. With MSK Replicator, you can easily build regionally resilient streaming applications for increased availability and business continuity. MSK Replicator provides automatic asynchronous replication across Kafka clusters, eliminating the need to write custom code, manage infrastructure, or setup cross-region networking. MSK Replicator automatically scales the underlying resources so that you can replicate data on-demand without having to monitor or scale capacity. MSK Replicator also replicates the necessary Kafka metadata including topic configurations, Access Control Lists (ACLs), and consumer group offsets. If an unexpected event occurs in a region, you can failover to the other AWS Region and seamlessly resume processing. You can get started with MSK Replicator from the Amazon MSK console or the Amazon CLI. To learn more, visit the MSK Replicator documentation , product page , and pricing page .
articles.summary: MSK Replicator d'AWS permet de répliquer automatiquement des données Kafka entre régions GovCloud pour une résilience et continuité métier sans gestion d'infrastructure.

articles.title: Amazon Redshift expands SUPER data type to store strings up to 16 million bytes
articles.excerpt: Amazon Redshift now supports individual strings up to 16 million bytes within SUPER data types . Once you opt in through a database parameter, this enhancement applies when ingesting structured or semi-structured data from JSON, PARQUET, TEXT, and CSV source files, and when transforming data through extract load and transform (ELT) processes. Previously, individual strings within SUPER data types were limited to 65,535 bytes. Storing large individual strings in the SUPER data type helps avoid complex pre-loading transformations needed to store the source data in Amazon Redshift. You can now directly ingest large individual strings greater than 65,535 bytes without extra processing (for example, lengthy documents like terms and conditions and contracts), making them queryable using SQL. Once the data is in Amazon Redshift, you can use the flexibility of PartiQL language to explore and navigate through the data or use string functions to transform the data. Functions such as JSON_PARSE , CONCAT , and LISTAGG can now take input strings and return output strings up to 16 million bytes in length. This enhancement is available in all AWS Regions, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, where Amazon Redshift is available. See the AWS Region Table for more details. To learn more, please visit our documentation or blog .
articles.summary: Amazon Redshift étend le type SUPER à 16 Mo pour stocker directement de longues chaînes (JSON, contrats) sans transformation préalable, simplifiant l'ingestion et les requêtes SQL.

articles.title: AWS launches support for amortization of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML
articles.excerpt: AWS Data Exports for Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 and AWS Cost Explorer now amortize the upfront fee for Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML across the duration of each reservation. You can see the amortized cost of each instance launched into a Capacity Block and the amortized cost of unused capacity, so you can attribute your upfront fee to the workloads that used it and identify capacity that went unused. Previously, a Capacity Block's upfront fee appeared as a single charge on the purchase date, making it difficult to see how that cost was spread across usage over the reservation. Now the amortized cost appears alongside your instance usage, so you can allocate GPU costs to the teams, projects, and applications that ran on the reserved capacity. You can also see what share of your reservation went unused and plan future Capacity Block purchases. In CUR 2.0, the amortized costs appear in the reservation_amortized_upfront_fee_for_billing_period, reservation_effective_cost columns, and reservation_net_effective_cost shows the amortized cost after discounts. In Cost Explorer, select the amortized cost view to see Capacity Block costs allocated for the reservation. Amortization for Capacity Blocks is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions. To learn more, see the CUR 2.0 data dictionary and exploring your data using Cost Explorer .
articles.summary: AWS amortit désormais les coûts des EC2 Capacity Blocks pour le ML, améliorant la visibilité et l'allocation des frais réservés aux workloads.

articles.title: Only include resource detectors you need by building your own Collector
articles.excerpt:
There are many reasons for building your own OpenTelemetry Collector
distribution. The existing distributions are designed to be broadly useful,
which means they include many more components than what an individual deployment
uses. Building your own gives you the ability to select only the components you
care about, add your own custom components, and control exactly what ends up in
the binary you run in production. 
 One of the reasons I prefer to build my own distribution is to limit the size of
the binary I have to ship around and to ensure that the least amount of
dependencies are included. Fewer dependencies means a smaller binary, a smaller
attack surface, and fewer third-party modules to track when a vulnerability is
disclosed. The
 OpenTelemetry Collector Builder (ocb) makes this
possible: you write a manifest file in YAML to select the components you care
about, and ocb compiles them into the resulting binary.
articles.summary: Construire son propre Collector OpenTelemetry réduit les dépendances, la taille du binaire et la surface d'attaque pour une sécurité optimisée en production.
